month.title: Programming fundamentals
month.theme: Move from copying code to decomposing problems and debugging deliberately.
month.mastery: Build a small application without following a tutorial step-by-step.
month.checkpoint: An interactive app that fetches real data, with loading and error states, a README, and one documented bug hunt.

weeks.title: JavaScript fundamentals
weeks.objective: Write small programs that take input, make decisions and produce output, and read error messages without panic.
learn: Values and types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined
Variables: const vs let, and why var is avoided
Operators and comparisons (=== vs ==)
Conditionals: if/else, the ternary operator, truthy and falsy
Loops: for, for…of, while
Functions: parameters, return values, scope
Reading errors in the console: message, file, line
practice: Write a function that converts a design spec in px to rem
Write FizzBuzz, then explain it line by line
Write a function that returns a greeting based on the hour of the day
Break your code on purpose in 3 ways and read each error message out loud

build.title: Tip & split calculator
build.brief: A small page where you enter a bill, a tip percentage and the number of people, and see each person's share. Handle empty and invalid input gracefully.

weeks.prove: Explain every line of your calculator to a rubber duck or a voice memo: what runs, in what order, and what each value is at each step.
reflect: Which error message confused you most, and what did it actually mean?
weeks.ship: Calculator committed with a README and deployed alongside your Week 4 site.

tryFirst.task: Write a function splitBill(total, tipPercent, people) that returns each person's share rounded to 2 decimals.
tryFirst.hint: Break it into steps: tip amount, grand total, per-person share, rounding. What should happen if people is 0?
tryFirst.explanation: Good functions do one job and guard their inputs. Guard clauses at the top handle bad input before the main logic. Rounding via cents keeps the result a number (toFixed would return a string).

weeks.title: Variables, data structures and functions
weeks.objective: Model real things as data (arrays of objects) and write functions that transform that data.
learn: Arrays: index, length, push, slice, includes
Objects: properties, nesting, destructuring
Arrays of objects: the shape of most app data
map, filter, find, reduce: transform instead of loop-and-mutate
Immutability: why you copy instead of change
Functions as values: callbacks and arrow functions
JSON: data as text
practice: Represent 5 of your design projects as an array of objects (title, year, tools, client)
Use reduce to count projects per year
Convert the array to JSON and back

build.title: Contact list
build.brief: A contact list app: add a contact (name, phone, tag), search by name, filter by tag, delete. Data lives in an array of objects, and every operation is a small named function.

weeks.prove: Change a requirement without starting over: add a 'favourite' flag and a 'favourites first' sort. Note how many functions you had to touch.
reflect: Where did you mutate data you should have copied?
weeks.ship: Contact list on GitHub with a README that shows your data shape.

tryFirst.task: Given contacts = [{ name, tag }], return a new array of only the 'client' contacts, sorted by name, without changing the original array.
tryFirst.hint: filter decides who stays. sort changes the array in place, so copy first (or use toSorted). localeCompare compares strings properly.
tryFirst.explanation: filter returns a new array; toSorted (or [...array].sort) avoids mutating the original. Chaining small transformations reads like a sentence: keep the clients, sort them by name.

weeks.title: DOM, events and interaction
weeks.objective: Connect data to the screen: render from state, react to events, and persist between visits.
learn: The DOM as a tree you can query and change
querySelector, createElement, textContent vs innerHTML (and why innerHTML with user input is dangerous)
Events: click, input, submit, keydown; event.preventDefault
Event delegation for lists
The render-from-state pattern: data changes, then the screen re-renders
localStorage: saving and loading JSON
Form handling and validation in the browser
practice: Render your projects array into cards with createElement
Add a live search that filters the cards as you type
Use event delegation to delete a card from a list
Persist a counter in localStorage so it survives a refresh

build.title: Personal expense tracker
build.brief: Add expenses (amount, category, date), see a running total and per-category totals, delete entries, and keep everything after a refresh. Render everything from one state array.

weeks.prove: Keyboard-only test: add, filter and delete an expense without touching the mouse. Fix whatever blocks you.
reflect: Where did your screen and your data get out of sync, and why?
weeks.ship: Expense tracker deployed, with an empty state, an error for invalid amounts, and a README.

tryFirst.task: Clicking 'Delete' on any expense in a list should remove that expense, using a single event listener for the whole list.
tryFirst.hint: Listen on the list, not on each button. The event knows which element was clicked (event.target). Put the expense id on the button as a data attribute.
tryFirst.explanation: Event delegation: one listener on a parent handles events from many children, including ones added later. closest() walks up to the element you care about, and data attributes carry the id back to your state.

resources.title: MDN · Using the Web Storage API

weeks.title: Async JavaScript, APIs and debugging
weeks.objective: Fetch real data, handle every state it can be in, and debug systematically instead of guessing.
learn: Synchronous vs asynchronous code: why the page doesn't freeze
Promises and async/await
fetch: request, response, response.ok, JSON parsing
Loading, success, empty and error states
Error handling with try/catch
API keys: why they never belong in browser code
Debugging: breakpoints, the Network panel, console.table
practice: Fetch a list from a public API (for example Open-Meteo) and log it
Show a loading message, then the data, then an error state when you go offline
Set a breakpoint inside your fetch handler and inspect the response
Write down your debugging steps for one real bug

build.title: Weather dashboard
build.brief: Search a city and show current conditions plus a 5-day forecast from a free, keyless API (Open-Meteo). Design every state: idle, loading, success, not found, network error.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: build an API-powered application without tutorial guidance.
reflect: What did you learn from the bug that took longest to fix?
weeks.ship: GitHub repository plus a README with screenshots of every state.

tryFirst.task: Fetch weather for given coordinates and show 'Could not load weather' if anything fails, including a non-200 response.
tryFirst.hint: fetch only rejects on network failure. A 404 or 500 still 'succeeds', so check response.ok yourself.
tryFirst.explanation: Wrap the request in try/catch, throw when !response.ok, and keep the UI states explicit. Always end in a state the user can see, never a silent failure.

mastery.title: Build an API-powered app without a tutorial
mastery.challenge: Build a small app that fetches data from a public API you haven't used before and lets the user search or filter it.
constraints: No step-by-step tutorial; official API docs and MDN are allowed
If you use AI, only to explain errors, not to write the app
criteria: Fetches real data and renders it from state
Loading, empty, error and success states are each visible
User input is validated and never inserted with innerHTML
No API keys in browser code
README explains the data flow and one bug you fixed
You can change one requirement live without starting over
